extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Coast Guard managers, contracting officers, procurement officials, policy analysts, and researchers studying OMB Circular A-76 implementation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of implementation, cost-comparison, and administration requirements under OMB Circular A-76 for U.S. Coast Guard commercial activities, including causes of contract cost increases and perceptions of the program. Focuses on PWS/MEO preparation, solicitation/award rules, post-award cost drivers, and oversight practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of 'Commercial Activities'
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of a Government agency's 'Commercial Activities' (with some exceptions given in the policy) that could be contracted out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Circular requires agencies to develop an inventory of commercial activities for A-76 consideration; examples of commercial activities include audiovisual, ADP services, food services, health services, maintenance/repair, security, transportation, printing, and others [34:p.7-10].

rubrics_metrics.name: Most Efficient Organization (MEO) determination
rubrics_metrics.description: From the PWS determine the best organizational structure and operating procedure for the function — the Most Efficient Organization (MEO) — and determine the cost of operating the function in-house under the MEO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MEO is intended to 'cut the fat' and encourage efficiency by reducing costs and personnel as necessary; MEO cost is used as the Government in-house cost for competition with private offerors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of Performance Work Statement (PWS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a Performance Work Statement (PWS) that describes what the function is and what it takes to do it; the PWS is used for solicitation and as the basis for MEO and contractor performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS should define the function by measurable work standards and focus on 'what' is required rather than 'how' to perform it; development of an accurate PWS is central to a valid cost comparison and subsequent contract administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Assurance (QA) plan within PWS
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a Quality Assurance (QA) plan as part of the PWS to ensure goods and services received from a contractor meet the PWS requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: QA plan describes Government actions to ensure contractor performance meets specification; inadequate QA planning contributes to post-award problems and service issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-comparison award rule (10 percent rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the total cost of contracting out is less than the MEO's cost by more than 10 percent of the MEO's personnel-related costs, and the offeror is determined responsible, then the activity is contracted-out; if the offeror's cost is within 10 percent of the MEO cost or greater than the MEO, the activity remains in-house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sealed bid process confidentiality is maintained so Government and contractor costs remain independent; contracting officer does not know in-house cost until bid opening [35:p.IV-3, IV-4].

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions allowing in-house retention
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities may remain in-house if they meet one of: no satisfactory commercial source available; national defense reasons (Secretary of Defense authorization); patient care (best interest of patient care or maintaining military medical capability); or Government performance costs are lower than a qualified commercial source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exemptions are explicit criteria under A-76 for retaining inherently governmental or otherwise excepted functions [34:p.4-5].

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-function (<10 FTE) fair & reasonable exception
rubrics_metrics.description: For functions having less than 10 full-time equivalents (FTE), a cost comparison is not required as long as the price is 'fair & reasonable'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Fair & reasonable' is determined based on sufficient competition in the service industry to induce fair prices [35:p.I-12].

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-round review requirement (five-year re-review)
rubrics_metrics.description: A second round review five years after the original study is required for all commercial activities retained in-house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to ensure continued appropriateness of in-house status; re-review can identify need to recompete or adjust MEO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sealed-bid confidentiality and solicitation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Most solicitations use Invitation for Bid (IFB)/sealed bid method; confidentiality of all cost data is maintained so contracting officer does not know in-house cost until bid opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sealed-bid is used because many service contracts compete primarily on price; some solicitations use RFP/negotiation depending on the PWS or set-asides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return-to-in-house/recompete thresholds and approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: To return an activity to in-house the MEO must better a private-sector offeror by a ten percent cost increment (described as twenty percent lower than the originally competed MEO cost) plus twenty-five percent of the contractor's capital assets cost; the agency Secretary must approve return to in-house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recompete or another cost-comparison may be initiated for unsatisfactory service or if contract costs become unreasonable; returning contracted-out functions is deliberately difficult to deter frequent reversals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of post-award contract cost increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary factors that contribute to contract cost increases following award include Department of Labor (DOL) wage determinations, food price increases, added work, and delay in follow-on contract award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some causes (DOL wage determinations, commodity price inflation) are outside contracting officer control; added work can be anticipated via adequate contract specifications but unexpected situations still create costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracting Officer's Technical Representative (COTR) role and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Need for a COTR to monitor contractor performance; typical COTRs serve short durations (2–3 years) and often receive limited training or experience in quality assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient COTR training and turnover can undermine contract oversight and contribute to service problems and cost escalations; improving COTR training/content is a recommended area for research and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 8(a)/small-business set-asides and effect on cost-comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: When activities are reserved for Small Business Administration Section 8(a) set-asides (or small business competitions), a formal cost comparison may not be required, facilitating contracting-out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserving work for 8(a) firms made contracting-out easier and helped meet SBA quotas; however, it can affect the rigor of cost-comparison and selection outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation funding/term expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bids or proposals are expected to be on at least a three-year basis for multi-year funding or cover two fiscal years after the initial year for single-year funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the expected contract term for cost comparisons and budget planning; multi-year basis affects contractor pricing and government cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that PWS specify measurable work standards (not 'how')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1979 A-76 revision introduced defining needs by measurable work standards and not by 'how' the activity is done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying 'what' rather than 'how' enables fair competition and allows contractors to propose efficient means of meeting performance standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of Government savings and effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Intended result of A-76 reviews is Government cost savings and a more efficient activity; savings should be measured in dollars and in increased efficiency/productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thesis compares contract costs with Government MEO to see if Government savings were still being realized; GAO and DOT reports critique completeness/accuracy of reported savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract administration and oversight responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts, after award, are administered by designated contract branches (e.g., MLCPAC) and require ongoing oversight to control costs and service quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective administration (timely recompete planning, QA enforcement, relationship with contractors) is necessary to prevent cost increases and service degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited opportunities for Coast Guard to control some cost drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracting officers cannot control DOL wage determinations or commodity price increases; added work can be mitigated by adequate specifications; delays in follow-on awards can be prevented by advance planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes boundaries of control and points to where improved specification, planning, and clauses (e.g., cost ceilings) could mitigate cost growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to include cost-ceiling clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate a cost ceiling clause in contracts set at a level to ensure contract cost stays below the MEO cost by the A-76 specified amount to ensure Government cost savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cost ceiling could limit contractor price growth and preserve the intended savings margin relative to MEO; MLCPAC suggested this as a cost-control mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for accurate, timely, and skilled management studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective A-76 studies require advanced planning, preparation, skill, and comprehensive analysis of the function; many studies are lengthy, inaccurate, and burdensome to the activity being studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poorly conducted studies and poorly written PWSs are a core problem identified by GAO and practitioners; improving study methods is critical to valid cost comparisons and outcomes.
